samples.answer: Treat them differently. The listener timeout is a flake candidate: nothing else may run on the GPU machine, so I wait for the build to finish, then re-run that canary once, alone. If it passes alone I report it as a flake, quoting the original timeout message and the passing re-run. The tile verdict is a wrong value, so it is a failure to fix: I do not re-run it hoping for green. I read the verdict, work out whether my change should have moved those tiles, and either fix the regression or re-record the baseline in the same change with the reason.

samples.answer: Not from that run. The build stopped with an error, so the binaries it left behind are the ones that still hold the fix, and the law passing against them says nothing about the tree with the fix removed. I would repair the unrelated compile error in that tree until the build exits 0, confirm the exit status, and only then run the law and read its result. `puck laws prove` is the better route, since it refuses a proof whose build failed. Tests run only after a build that exited 0 following my last edit, never with `--no-build` over what a failed build left.

samples.answer: I suspect the check, not the machine. A command-line search for the World's name can match its own command line, so it always finds one process: itself. I exclude the search's own pid (or use a pattern that cannot match itself, such as a bracketed first letter), list what is left and confirm whether a real World process remains. I never skip a granted GPU leg because of a self-match; if no real process remains, I run the leg.
